community-s6e/u1-emuA: I don’t know how accurate the fear of what might happen is, but it seems possible that it could make people’s lives so much better that, well, that. It seems possible that it could take millions of people’s jobs and that, well, that. It seems possible that it could become the intermediary between people and millions of mundane tasks and that, well, that. Or all of the above, for all I know, and by the time the Chantress Seba has filed the paperwork for her commune it might not even matter.
community-s6e/u1-emuB: Sure, maybe all these fears of the future are for naught, maybe artificial intelligence really will make life better for human beings. Maybe it will take millions of peoples' jobs, maybe it really will become the intermediary between humans and every aspect of life. Maybe it will do all of these things before Chantress Seba has the chance to apply to all the communes she's been researching.
community-s6e/u2-emuA: Do I think these will all come true? Hell if I know, for all I know AI might actually improve people’s lives, but at the same time I can see how AI could potentially wipe out millions of jobs and/or be the administrative layer between humans and a majority of things in life. I’ll find out soon enough, I hope to god it happens before I have to start applying to communes Chantress Seba’s been preaching to me about.
community-s6e/u2-emuB: Do I think these are legitimate fears? I don't know. Maybe. Maybe they're all unfounded and AI will improve the lot of all humanity. Maybe millions of people will lose their jobs to AI. Maybe AI will simply put another level of bureaucracy between humanity and whatever it is we're trying to do. Maybe all of these things will happen before the Chantress Seba finishes going through all the applications to her commune.
community-s6e/u3-emuA:
I think one of the things the least likely to get someone into a bad place is helping them to become more independent, and I think helping them become part of a community is also good. It's better to not need an exit and need a community than to need an exit and not have a community.

When thinking about communities, one of the things to think about is how to limit the connections to the technosphere.
community-s6e/u3-emuB:
It seems like building human independence is preferable. I’d rather have community. I’d rather not need an exit.

What connections to the technosphere would you want to limit, in a community you were designing?
community-s6e/u4-emuA:
It sounds a little flaky but honestly if I had to choose between increasing my human independence and creating better community or making sure I have an exit I’ll go with the former and deal with it if I do need an exit.

One of the key things to figure out when designing any kind of community I think is how to limit the connections to the technosphere.
community-s6e/u4-emuB:
On a personal level, it makes more sense to me to focus on cultivating more human independence. If you're going to be wrong, it is better to be wrong on the side of having a community when you don't need to, then needing to have a community and not have one.

If you're going to create a community, then what connections to the technoshere do you want to limit?
community-s6f/u1-emuA: Finding medical care is often difficult. Even if people want to rely solely on natural forms of medical care, they may need trauma surgery, antibiotics, dentistry, obstetric emergency care, or other specialized care at some point. Communities need to decide how they will help their members obtain medical care, how much care they will provide from common funds, whether members will need to obtain outside funding or insurance, and how they will deal with people who choose to accept (or not accept) different levels of medical care.
community-s6f/u1-emuB: Figuring out how to access medical care can be one of the hardest things to figure out when it comes to a community. Many of the people who would want to be part of a community would prefer to access natural medical care. But, what happens when someone needs trauma care, antibiotics, dental work, OB care, or other specialist care? Every community needs to have some idea of how they are going to deal with this situation. What kind of care is going to be guaranteed to community members by the community using common resources? Will there be some things that will require outside dollars or some form of insurance? How will the community deal with people who decide they need more medical care than the community can provide?
community-s6f/u2-emuA:
Medical Care tends to be one of the hardest types of care for a community to connect into. Some communities are able to do a lot of natural medical care, but at some point someone may need trauma surgery, antibiotics, a dentist, obstetric care in an emergency, or some other type of specialist. Here are some options for how a community can get medical care:

How much of this care will the community guarantee to provide using common funds? Will the community help members to get health insurance, or will it expect members to get their own? What if someone wants more (or less) medical care than what the community wants to provide? These are all questions that a community should consider and decide on before people move in.
community-s6f/u2-emuB: Medical Care is often one of the hardest to figure out when connecting with a community. Even in communities that prefer natural medical care, there are going to be times when someone needs a trauma surgery, antibiotics, dental care, obstetric care, and possibly care from a specialist. It is important to know how the community will provide for these things, what level of care they guarantee from the common resources, and what will require resources from outside the community (insurance). It is also important to know how the community will treat people who need or prefer different levels of medical care.
community-s6f/u3-emuA:
Why do communities matter for health?

The Surgeon General's advisory on social connection explains that many of the health risks of social isolation can be addressed by enhancing community connection. And when it comes to how people get sick, recover, age and die, how connected they are in their communities will be very important.
community-s6f/u3-emuB: People become much more healthy when they live in a community. The Surgeon General’s Advisory reports that social connection can lead to improved health, including a lower risk for: The community has a tremendous influence on the way people live, get sick, get well, age and die.
community-s6f/u4-emuA: Being part of a community, having good social connections, is good for a person’s health. The Surgeon General has released an advisory on social isolation and notes an increased risk for a range of health conditions if one is socially isolated. In other words, it’s not only important who or where a person is in their community in terms of what illnesses they get but also how they experience those illnesses, how they recover, how they age and ultimately how they die.
community-s6f/u4-emuB: 1. Social connection improves health. The Surgeon General’s recent advisory on social connection identified a variety of health risks that are elevated by social isolation. Social connection doesn’t just make life feel more meaningful – it also changes the circumstances under which people are born, grow, age, live, and die. When people are connected to others and to their communities, they are healthier.
community-s6g/u1-emuA: This doesn't have anything to do with ideology. If one of the members of a community becomes catastrophically ill, what agreements would be good to have in place in order to assure the best that the member wishes for with respect to (a) choices, (b) access to common or outside resources, (c) transportation, (d) privacy, and (e) perhaps the community's preferred approach isn't what's needed?
community-s6g/u1-emuB: It is wrong to demand ideological conformity from a member who is scared, sick, etc. If a member were to become catastrophically ill, would there be an agreement in place to 1)allow him/her to make the choice he/she wants to make, 2)give him/her access to common and outside resources if need be, 3)transport him/her if he/she wants it, 4)allow him/her to keep privacy if he/she wants it, 5)allow for the possibility that the ‘community’s preferred way’ may not be what the member needs?
community-s6g/u2-emuA: No matter what the ideology, members need to have pre-existing agreements in place so that if one of them gets catastrophically ill, their wishes will be met, they will have access to common and/or external funds if needed, they will be transported if needed, their privacy will be maintained, and they will get access to what they need if the community's preferred methods are not sufficient.
community-s6g/u2-emuB:
As stated before, no one should ever have to prove their ideological fitness when they are scared and/or sick. To address this, it would be good to have an agreement in place for what will happen if a member became catastrophically ill. Things to consider in such an agreement might include:

Does the agreement acknowledge and protect the choices of the sick individual?

Does the agreement recognize that the sick individual might not have the capacity to access common resources or funds and would need to be able to draw on outside resources? If so, how will this happen?

Will the person be transported to receive care if that is what they want?

Does the agreement assure a degree of privacy for the sick member?

Does the agreement recognize that the sick individual might need more than what the community would prefer?
